Summary

A lightweight email service that triggers Plunk templates for transactional emails. Email design/copy stays in Plunk; the backend only triggers the right template with the recipient's name and link.

Variable Purpose

  • SendPasswordResetEmail(toEmail, name, link string) error — triggers the reset template.

Both POST to Plunk /v1/track with { event, email, data: { name, link } }. An unconfigured template name returns a clear error; a non-2xx response surfaces the status.

  • Verification template name comes from an environment variable (PLUNK_VERIFY_TEMPLATE), not hardcoded
  • Reset template name comes from a separate environment variable (PLUNK_RESET_TEMPLATE)
  • Service passes the user's name and full link URL to the email platform (asserted in tests via a capturing HTTP server)

Verification

  • go test ./src/services/ — 2 tests pass (TDD: failing first, then implemented). Tests use httptest to capture and assert the outgoing request (auth header, event name from env, email, data.name, data.link).

Notes for Reviewer

  • Plunk integration uses the event trigger endpoint (/v1/track); the configured template name is sent as the event that drives the Plunk automation/template. Confirm this matches the Plunk setup (vs. the raw /v1/send transactional endpoint).
  • data payload carries name and link — confirm these match the variable names used inside the Plunk templates.
  • PLUNK_API_KEY must be set in deployment; left blank in local .env for now.

Task 4: Automated Email Sending

Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-backend-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-backend-plan.md

Context

GoThru needs to send two types of transactional emails to users: an email verification link after signup, and a password reset link when requested. These emails are not designed or written in code — their design and copy live in the Plunk email platform. The backend's only job is to trigger the right template with the right data.

Goal

Build the email-sending service that the auth handlers call when they need to send a verification or reset email.

What We're Building

A lightweight email service that:

  • Connects to the Plunk email platform using a secret API key stored in the environment
  • Sends a verification email by triggering the correct Plunk template and passing in the recipient's name and their unique verification link
  • Sends a password reset email by triggering a different Plunk template with the recipient's name and their unique reset link
  • Uses template names configured via environment variables — no email content is hardcoded

Why It Matters

Without this service, users who register cannot verify their email, and users who forget their password are locked out permanently. This is a required piece of the signup and recovery flows.

Acceptance Criteria

  • The service builds and compiles without errors
  • The template name used for verification emails comes from an environment variable, not hardcoded text
  • The template name used for reset emails comes from a separate environment variable
  • The service passes the user's name and the full link URL to the email platform

What Changes After This Task

The registration handler (Task 6) can send verification emails on signup. The forgot-password handler can send reset emails on request.

src/middleware/auth.go

This is the core of the protection layer. The Auth() middleware performs the following steps before the request ever reaches the controller:

  2. Token Verification: Passes the token to utils.VerifySessionToken(token), which decodes the JWT and validates its signature and expiration against the JWT_SECRET. It returns the user's unique_id.

func (ac *AuthController) Me(c *fiber.Ctx) error {

The forgot-password flow is implemented to prioritize security, particularly against user enumeration and email spam. It uses a one-time token (OTP) architecture backed by the otps database table.

src/controllers/v1/auth/forgotPassword.go

src/action/v1/auth/forgotPassword.go

This action contains the core business logic and strict security constraints:

  1. User Lookup (Anti-Enumeration):
    It queries the users table for the provided email (converted to lowercase). If the user is not found (or is soft-deleted), the function silently returns nil (success). This is a critical OWASP best practice to prevent User Enumeration attacks.
  2. Spam Prevention (Cooldown):
    If the user exists, it checks the otps table for an existing reset_password token for that user. If the token was updated less than 60 seconds ago, it rejects the request with a "please wait 1 minute" error, mapping to a 429 Too Many Requests status.
  3. Token Generation:
    Calls utils.GenerateOneTimeToken() which generates a high-entropy string (raw token) and its SHA-256 hash.
  4. Token Storage:
    Calls UpsertOTP to store the hashed token in the database, setting its expiration to exactly 15 minutes from the current time.
  5. Background Email Dispatch:
    Constructs the reset link using the FRONTEND_URL and the raw token. It then fires go emailService.SendPasswordResetEmail(...) asynchronously. By using a goroutine, the API can immediately respond to the user without waiting for the network latency of the Plunk email API.

Security Highlights

  • No Plaintext Tokens: The database only stores the SHA-256 hash of the token. Even if the database is compromised, the attacker cannot use the tokens to reset passwords.
  • Anti-Enumeration: The response is identical whether the user exists or not.
  • Soft Delete Awareness: Accounts marked as deleted (deleted_at != NULL) are treated as non-existent by GORM and will silently succeed without sending an email.

The reset password API finalizes the account recovery process. It ensures the integrity of the password change by strictly validating the token and employing a database transaction to prevent token reuse (replay attacks).

src/controllers/v1/auth/resetPassword.go

This action performs the highly-sensitive operation of updating user credentials:

  1. Password Validation: Immediately rejects the request if the password is less than 8 characters long.
  2. Token Verification:
    • Hashes the raw token using utils.HashToken().
    • Queries the otps table for a record matching the hashed token, where type is models.OTPTypeResetPassword, and expires_at is greater than time.Now().
    • If not found or expired, it returns ErrInvalidToken.
  3. Password Hashing: Hashes the new plaintext password using bcrypt via utils.HashPassword().

    • Step 2: Deletes the OTP record from the otps table so it can never be used again.
    • If either step fails, the transaction rolls back, preventing a state where the password is changed but the token remains active (or vice versa).

  • Replay Attack Prevention: The token is strictly deleted in the same atomic transaction as the password update.
  • Timing Attacks: Token comparisons are safely deferred to the database engine using hashed values.
  • Bcrypt: New passwords are appropriately salted and hashed.

Context

All the individual pieces — database connection, error handling, auth helpers, email service, middleware, auth handlers, project handlers — have been built in isolation. This task is where they all come together into a single running service that can accept real HTTP requests.

Goal

Write the entry point of the backend service: the code that starts up, connects to the database, wires every route to its handler, applies the right security rules, and begins listening for requests.

What We're Building

The main server file that:

  • Starts the database connection on startup
  • Creates all handler instances (auth, projects) and gives them access to the database
  • Sets up CORS (cross-origin) rules so only the GoThru website domain can call the API
  • Registers every route under /v1/ with the correct HTTP method
  • Applies the auth gate to all protected routes, leaving public routes (login, register, etc.) open
  • Exposes a /health endpoint for monitoring tools to confirm the service is running
  • Reads the port from an environment variable (defaulting to 8080)

Why It Matters

Without this file, all the individual handlers are unreachable — they exist as code but respond to nothing. This is the task that makes the backend a real, working service that the website can call.

Acceptance Criteria

  • The service starts without errors when a database is available
  • GET /health returns "ok"
  • All project and file endpoints reject requests without a valid session token
  • All auth endpoints (login, register, forgot-password) are accessible without a token
  • Requests to non-existent routes return 404 cleanly

The backend is fully operational. The website can now be pointed at it and all auth and project flows will work end to end.
